strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea of training on random toy compositions for generalization, grounded in developmental psychology and Cézanne's compositional principle
Comprehensive experimental scope spanning simulation, multiple real robot platforms (Franka Panda, Unitree H1-2), and multiple baselines
Extensive reproducibility documentation in appendices with detailed 3D printing settings, hardware configurations, and implementation details
Thoughtful ablation studies examining scaling laws, toy diversity effects, model size impact, and primitive importance
Practical demonstration of zero-shot transfer from toy training to real robot grasping tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Detection pooling is a straightforward application of SAM2 + mean pooling; architecture uses standard ViT encoder and transformer policy. Main contribution is dataset design, not algorithmic innovation

Unfair and problematic baseline comparisons: π₀-FAST and OpenVLA-OFT compared against versions trained on different data regimes (DROID pretraining, large-scale robot data) rather than the same toy dataset as LEGO, making it impossible to isolate the contribution of the toy dataset itself
Overstated claims: Title claims 'grasp anything' but results show only 67% on YCB and 50.77% on H1-2; abstract claims 'robust generalization' despite marginal improvements (2-3%) over baselines
Weak real-world validation: Only 13 everyday objects tested on H1-2; 50.77% success rate is modest; technical issues (unresponsive thumb joints) limited evaluation scope

Limited insight into generalization mechanism: No analysis of why toy shapes transfer to real objects, what visual features are learned, or which failure modes correlate with object properties not in training data
Evaluation methodology lacks statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; success rates reported as single numbers without variance estimates

Possible evaluation set bias: YCB objects likely have inherent bias toward primitive shapes (cubes, cylinders); no evidence provided that performance on objects NOT decomposable into 4 primitives is comparable

Incomplete ablations: Table 4 shows removing sphere only drops performance ~6%, inconsistent with claims that all 4 primitives are critical; missing ablation of training competing methods on same toy dataset
Scope limitations: Only single-step grasping addressed; no multi-step manipulation or alternative interaction modes limits practical applicability and generality claims
Missing computational analysis: No inference time reported; DetPool requires SAM2 + mask annotation with unspecified overhead; scalability to more complex primitives not addressed

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach: Using random compositions of geometric primitives for manipulation learning is creative, grounded in cognitive science and art history, and demonstrates an elegant path to scalable generalization.

Strong technical contribution: Detection pooling (DeiPool) is a principled mechanism for extracting object-centric visual representations, with clear ablation support showing its importance for zero-shot generalization.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multi-platform evaluation (simulation, real Franka, H1-2 humanoid) with proper baselines, thorough ablations examining demonstrations, toy diversity, model size, primitives, and complexity, providing genuine insights into scaling laws.

Impressive data efficiency: Achieves competitive performance with 1,500 demonstrations, significantly outperforming methods like OpenVLA-OFT and comparable to π₀-FAST in zero-shot setting, demonstrating practical efficiency.
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware configurations, and commitment to release code and dataset enable reproduction and follow-up work.

Honest and clear presentation: Paper clearly articulates contributions, provides thorough implementation details in appendices, acknowledges limitations explicitly, and uses effective figures and ablation tables to support claims.
weaknesses: Limited real-world evaluation scope: Only 64 out of full YCB objects tested (selected as 'feasibly graspable'), and H1-2 real robot evaluation on just 13 everyday objects. No testing on objects fundamentally different from geometric shapes (deformable objects, cloth, thin/elongated items). This partially contradicts the ambitious title 'Learning to Grasp Anything.'

Performance gap with best baseline: π₀-FAST with finetuning achieves 76.56% vs. method's 66.67% on YCB. While paper argues π₀-FAST requires more diverse data, this limits practical advantage claims and suggests the approach trades some performance for data efficiency.

Narrow task scope: Limited to single-step grasping without multi-step manipulation, sequential planning, or dynamic tasks. This substantially limits immediate practical impact despite being acknowledged as future work.

Insufficient failure analysis: Limited discussion of which object categories fail, why, or systematic failure modes. Table 7 shows color diversity boosts performance 1-4%, suggesting reliance on visual cues beyond pure geometry, but this is not deeply explored.

H1-2 humanoid evaluation concerns: Technical issues with unresponsive thumb joints limit scope. 50.77% success rate is notably lower than Franka (66.67%) with insufficient analysis of causes. Small test set (13 objects) limits statistical significance.

Incomplete design justification: Primitive selection (4 types), dimension ranges (Table 6), and random generation process appear somewhat arbitrary. Limited ablation exploring alternative design choices or whether structured/optimized primitives might work better.

Computational cost under-explored: Paper mentions computational challenges but provides no detailed timing comparisons with baselines, memory requirements, or analysis of hardware constraints for deployment.

strengths: Creative core insight that complex objects can be learned from simple primitive compositions, well-motivated by cognitive science
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across simulation and multiple real robot platforms with extensive ablation studies
Strong empirical results demonstrating competitive performance to much larger models while using significantly fewer demonstrations (1,500 vs larger datasets)
Excellent reproducibility: promises code, checkpoints, datasets, and provides extensive implementation details in appendices
Thorough robustness analysis examining lighting variation, scene clutter, distractors, and mask noise
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of the approach and experimental results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Detection pooling is a relatively simple mechanism (SAM2 + attention masking + mean pooling), and overall architecture is standard. Novelty primarily lies in dataset/application design rather than methodological advancement

Overstated generalization claims: Title 'Learning to Grasp Anything' is hyperbolic; evaluation limited to 64 YCB objects and 13 everyday items. Geometric analysis (Table 6) shows significant performance variation (75.6-83.0%) across difficulty levels
Substantial and inadequately analyzed simulation-to-reality gap: 80% in simulation but only 66.67% on real Franka and 50.77% on H1-2, undermining claims about robust real-world generalization

Weak ablation of DetPool mechanism: Core claim that 'object-centric visual representation is key' lacks strong empirical support. Comparison with alternatives (mean/attention pooling) mentioned only briefly in Table 1

Questionable baseline comparisons: π₀-FAST and OpenVLA-OFT trained on different data/objectives; limited comparisons with other object-centric approaches beyond GROOT in appendix; no supervised learning baseline

Incomplete analysis: No systematic failure mode analysis, limited explanation of why sphere is most critical primitive, insufficient investigation of what object properties enable/prevent generalization
Limited task scope: Focused primarily on single-object grasping; push-to-target relegated to appendix; no multi-step manipulation, bin picking, or heavy clutter evaluation

Dataset limitations: Only 250 unique toys with 1,500 demonstrations; primitives are basic geometric shapes that may not capture complex real-world features; limited diversity in sizes, textures, and materials
Fragility to segmentation quality: Table 11 shows concerning 3% performance drop at 60% IoU, suggesting dependence on SAM2 mask quality; scalability of manual annotation requirement unclear

Missing analysis of core mechanisms: Why does learning from primitives enable generalization? Is it shape coverage, size invariance, or feature composition? Geometric similarity analysis provides hints but not definitive insights

strengths: Well-motivated approach grounded in cognitive science with creative use of simple primitives for generalizable learning
Exceptional experimental rigor with comprehensive evaluation across three distinct robot platforms (ManiSkill simulation, Franka, H1-2 humanoid)
Extensive ablation studies and scaling analysis providing clear insights into what drives generalization (primitives, data scale, model size, robustness factors)
Strong simulation results significantly outperforming baselines (80% vs 12.79% for OpenVLA-OFT with 2500 demos)
Exemplary reproducibility efforts with detailed appendices covering hardware, print settings, hyperparameters, and promised code release
Practical value: learning from synthetic toy compositions is more scalable than collecting diverse real-world objects
Thorough robustness analysis demonstrating performance stability under lighting variation, clutter, distractors, and mask noise
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, particularly Figure 1 communicating the core contribution
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: detection pooling is straightforward (mean pooling over SAM-segmented patches), and architecture is standard (ViT + transformer)
Real-world results less exceptional than claimed: Table 2 shows finetuned π₀-FAST achieves 76.56% vs LEGO's 66.67% on Franka with same pretraining, undercutting superiority claims
Baseline comparisons raise concerns: π₀-FAST achieves implausibly low 4.13% on 2500 synthetic demos, and different baselines use different pretraining data, making fair comparison unclear
Insufficient analysis of generalization mechanisms: unclear whether primitive shapes specifically enable generalization or if the benefit is primarily from increased data diversity
Missing critical experiment: comparison between training on real objects with perfect segmentation masks vs. primitive shapes to isolate the contribution of primitives
Limited real-world evaluation scope: tested only on YCB dataset (standard rigid objects) and 13 everyday items; no evaluation on challenging scenarios (cloth, occlusion, non-rigid objects)
Data efficiency claims require nuance: despite 'few-shot' framing, requires 1500 real demonstrations for Franka and 375K synthetic demonstrations (250 toys × 1500 each)
Insufficient depth on generalization limits: limited evidence method generalizes beyond rigid single-step grasping; no failure case analysis provided
Experimental design: Out-of-distribution evaluation less meaningful since training already includes randomly composed toys creating inherent OOD variation
Architectural choices under-explored: no justification or ablation for transformer policy choice; model scaling saturates at 86M parameters suggesting potential over-parameterization
